    "mcp>=2.2.0,<3.0.0",
    "pydantic>=2.13.0,<3.0.0",
    "lark>=1.3.1,<2.0.0",
]

[project.scripts]
specify = "specify_cli:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/specify_cli"]

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]
# Bundle core assets so `specify init` works without network access (air-gapped / enterprise)
# Page templates (exclude commands/ — bundled separately below to avoid duplication)
"templates/checklist-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/checklist-template.md"
"templates/constitution-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/constitution-template.md"
"templates/plan-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/plan-template.md"
"templates/spec-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/spec-template.md"
"templates/tasks-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/tasks-template.md"
"templates/vscode-settings.json" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/vscode-settings.json"
# Command templates
"templates/commands" = "specify_cli/core_pack/commands"
"scripts/bash" = "specify_cli/core_pack/scripts/bash"
"scripts/powershell" = "specify_cli/core_pack/scripts/powershell"
"scripts/python" = "specify_cli/core_pack/scripts/python"
# Bundled extensions (installable via `specify extension add <name>`)
"extensions/git" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/git"
"extensions/agent-context" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/agent-context"
"extensions/assess" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/assess"
"extensions/bug" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/bug"
"extensions/github" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/github"
# Bundled workflows (`specify init` installs only `speckit`; `bugfix`/`assess` are opt-in via first-party bundles)
"workflows/speckit" = "specify_cli/core_pack/workflows/speckit"
"workflows/bugfix" = "specify_cli/core_pack/workflows/bugfix"
"workflows/assess" = "specify_cli/core_pack/workflows/assess"
# Bundled presets (installable via `specify preset add <name>` or `specify init --preset <name>`)
"presets/lean" = "specify_cli/core_pack/presets/lean"
"presets/constitution-sync" = "specify_cli/core_pack/presets/constitution-sync"
# Bundle catalog snapshots (used for offline discovery)
"bundles/catalog.json" = "specify_cli/core_pack/bundles/catalog.json"
"bundles/catalog.community.json" = "specify_cli/core_pack/bundles/catalog.community.json"

[project.optional-dependencies]
test = [
    "cryptography",
    "pytest>=7.0",
    "pytest-cov>=4.0",
    "pytest-xdist>=3.0",
]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
python_files = ["test_*.py"]
python_classes = ["Test*"]
python_functions = ["test_*"]
addopts = [
    "-v",
    "--strict-markers",
    "--tb=short",
]

[tool.coverage.run]
source = ["src"]
omit = ["*/tests/*", "*/__pycache__/*"]

[tool.coverage.report]
precision = 2
show_missing = true
skip_covered = false

[tool.ruff.lint]
# Lock in subprocess security posture: any reintroduction of shell=True
# (or os.system / popen2) must be acknowledged with an explicit `# noqa`
# pointing at the rule, making the deviation visible in review.
extend-select = [
    "S602",  # subprocess-popen-with-shell-equals-true
    "S604",  # call-with-shell-equals-true
    "S605",  # start-process-with-a-shell
]

name: paper-orchestra
description: PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing.
readme_content:
#
🎻 PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing
Yiwen Song1, Yale Song1, Tomas Pfister1, and Jinsung Yoon1
1Google Cloud AI Research


PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers.
## Key Features - **Multi-Agent Pipeline**: Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. - **Comprehensive Literature Synthesis**: Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript. - **Visuals Generation**: Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams. - **LaTeX Automation**: Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates. ## Installation 1. **Environment Setup**: The project relies on a Conda environment named `paper_orchestra`. You can set up a similar environment with Python 3.11 and install the required dependencies. ```bash conda create -n paper_orchestra python=3.11 conda activate paper_orchestra pip install -r requirements.txt ``` 2. **Environment Variables**: Create a `.env` file in the root of the project and add your API keys: ```env # Add keys if you have them, otherwise leave them empty # You need to specify related keys if you want to use the model # For example, if you want to use Gemini models, you need to specify either VERTEX_AI_PROJECT and VERTEX_AI_LOCATION, or GEMINI_API_KEY # If you want to use OpenAI models, you need to specify OPENAI_API_KEY SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY=your_semantic_scholar_api_key OPENAI_API_KEY=your_openai_api_key VERTEX_AI_PROJECT=your_vertex_ai_project VERTEX_AI_LOCATION=your_vertex_ai_location GEMINI_API_KEY=your_gemini_api_key # if you want to run demo and send emails to yourself at the end, set these 2 fields as well SMTP_EMAIL=your_email SMTP_PASSWORD=your_password ``` ## Dataset The dataset used for paper generation is **not included** in this code repository. It will be released separately at a later date. Once available, you should download the dataset and place it under the `datasets/` directory. ## Usage You can run the paper generation pipeline using the provided bash script or directly via the Python CLI. ### Using the Bash Script ```bash ./paper_writing_cli.sh ``` ### Using the Python CLI directly ```bash python paper_writing_cli.py \ --raw_materials_dir /path_to_your_raw_materials/ \ --latex_template_dir /path_to_your_latex_template/ \ --output_dir /path_to_your_output_folder/ \ --use_plotting true ``` ### Key Arguments * `--raw_materials_dir`: (Required) Directory containing the raw materials (e.g., idea and experimental log). * `--latex_template_dir`: (Required) Directory containing the LaTeX template (e.g., `templates/cvpr2025`). * `--output_dir`: Directory to output the generated paper. If not specified, an automatic folder with a timestamp is created. * `--use_plotting`: Enable the plotting agent workflow to generate figures from code (Default: `False`). * `--writer_model_name`: LLM for writer and literature agents. * `--reflection_model_name`: LLM for reflection agents. ### Interactive Demo We provide an interactive Streamlit demo for the paper generation pipeline. For instructions on how to run and use it, please refer to the [README.md](frontend/README.md) in the `frontend` directory. ## Project Structure * `autoraters/`: Contains scripts for automated evaluation. * `methods/`: Core logic for agents and pipeline execution. * `templates/`: LaTeX templates for target conferences, you can add your own template by creating a new subfolder under this directory. * `utils/`: Utility functions for API calls, PDF handling, etc. ## Citation If you find this repo or our paper helpful, please cite it as follows: ```bibtex @article{song2026paperorchestra, title={PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing}, author={Song, Yiwen and Song, Yale and Pfister, Tomas and Yoon, Jinsung}, journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05018}, year={2026} } ``` # Disclaimer This is not an officially supported Google product.

name: rtk
description: CLI proxy that reduces LLM token consumption by 60-90% on common dev commands. Single Rust binary, zero dependencies
readme_content:
The cost reduction engine for AI coding agents.
Install it and forget it, then go as far as you want with pipelines.

Install • Pipelines • Docs • Website • RTK Pro • Discord

English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português


**① Install & forget: up to 90% less command output.** Test runs, diffs, logs and builds are compressed before your agent reads them. 100+ commands, under 25 ms per command, no config, nothing changes in how you work. `rtk gain` shows what you saved. **② Go further with pipelines, as far as you take it.** Hand heavy reads to a cheaper model, compress more than bash, clean the API traffic without breaking the prompt cache. One agent-agnostic file: start from a built-in, install one someone shared, or write and share your own. The community built the bash compressor 85k developers starred. Now it is building pipelines: the best one listed today cuts total cost by 20.2% in its [author's benchmark](https://www.rtk-ai.app/pipelines/). **Agents across the whole company?** [RTK Pro](https://pro.rtk-ai.app) is the control layer for every AI agent: one gateway for every AI call, costs, secrets and personal data, policies, team catalog, audit. [Discover RTK Pro ↓](#agents-across-the-whole-company-know-what-they-cost-what-they-touch-and-who-ran-what)


---
## Install & forget **macOS, and Linux with Homebrew** ```bash brew install rtk ``` **Windows, with winget** ```bash winget install rtk-ai.rtk ``` **Linux, macOS, WSL, or Git Bash on Windows, with the install script** ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh ``` **Then plug it into your agent** ```bash rtk init -g # Claude Code; every other agent: see "Works in your agent" ``` Restart your agent. That's it: when it runs `git status`, RTK runs `rtk git status` and the agent reads a 3-line summary instead of 40 lines. Nothing to learn, nothing to call, and upgrading RTK never changes this. > Another project named "rtk" exists on crates.io. Check you have this one: `rtk gain` must show the savings dashboard, not "command not found". > > Cargo, pre-built binaries, native Windows, WSL and uninstall: **[Installation guide](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/installation/)** · per-agent setup and `--dry-run`: **[Quick Start](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/quick-start/)**
## Measure it: `rtk gain` Every command RTK touches is counted on your machine. One command shows what it saved, today and since you installed it. ```bash rtk gain # Summary stats rtk gain --graph # ASCII graph (last 30 days) rtk gain --history # Recent command history rtk gain --daily # Day-by-day breakdown rtk gain --all --format json # JSON export for dashboards rtk discover # Find missed savings opportunities rtk discover --all --since 7 # All projects, last 7 days rtk session # Show RTK adoption across recent sessions ``` **What the numbers mean.** The compressor reduces the **command output** your agent reads, which is one part of the input tokens, which are one part of the bill: a 90% cut in command output is not a 90% cut in cost. Token counts are estimated as `bytes / 4`, so the percentages are reliable and the absolute numbers are approximate. After a week of data, `rtk gain` ends with one line about RTK Pro, at most once a day and only on a terminal. `pro_hint = false` under `[display]` in `config.toml` turns it off. > Full explanation: [How RTK Savings Work](docs/guide/resources/savings-explained.md) · attribution, the live dashboard and export formats: **[Token Savings Analytics](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/analytics/gain/)**
## Out of the box: the bash compressor The part 85k developers starred. Built by 200+ contributors, written against real command output, and every filter has to cut at least 20% to ship.

| Operation | What the agent reads | |-----------|----------------------| | `cargo test` / `npm test` / `pytest` / `go test` | Failures only, with their assertion; passing tests collapsed to a count | | `git status` / `git diff` / `git log` | Compact status, reduced diff context, one line per commit | | `git add/commit/push` | A confirmation line instead of progress output | | `ls` / `tree` / `grep` / `rg` | Trees with counts, matches grouped by file, long lines cut | | `ruff check` / `eslint` / `cargo clippy` | Grouped by rule and file | | `docker ps` / `kubectl` | Essential fields only | 100+ commands across Git, GitHub CLI, Cargo/Rust, JavaScript (npm, pnpm, vitest, jest, tsc, Next.js, Angular, Playwright, Prisma), Python (ruff, pytest, mypy, pip), Go (go test, golangci-lint), Ruby, .NET, JVM (Gradle, Maven), PHP, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, and the file/search builtins. Every command and its filter: **[What RTK Optimizes](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/what-rtk-covers/)** **Three promises** - **Never blocks.** If a filter fails, you get the raw output, and the command's exit code is passed through unchanged. - **Never worse.** RTK never prints more than the command did. - **Nothing hidden.** Output that is cut says where the full version is, and `rtk bypass` runs any command unfiltered, still tracked in `rtk gain`: ```bash rtk bypass git log --oneline -20 # full git log, no truncation rtk bypass npm install express # raw npm output ``` The hook rewrites shell commands. Built-in tools such as `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` pass through untouched out of the box; in Claude Code, a pipeline compresses them too (see [Pipelines](#want-to-go-further-pipelines) below). > **Does RTK break the prompt cache?** No: output is filtered once, before it enters the conversation. [Details](docs/guide/resources/troubleshooting.md#does-rtk-break-claudes-prompt-cache).
## Want to go further? Pipelines. Out of the box, RTK compresses command output and stops there. A pipeline is how you ask it for more: one small file that tells RTK what to do with what your agent reads and sends. No file means the compressor above and nothing else; a pipeline adds one thing at a time, and you can take it back out.

**What people turn on first** - **Compress everything the agent reads**, not just shell output: grep results, web pages, lockfiles, any output RTK has no filter for (Claude Code). - **Hand big file reads to a cheaper model** you choose. The file never enters your agent's context (Claude Code, with your API key). - **Clean the API traffic** your agent re-sends every turn, with the prompt cache kept intact (through the optional proxy, below). - **Make the agent write less**: terse prose, with code, paths, commands and errors kept in full (every agent). Each of these is a built-in pipeline, one line to turn on. **[rtk-ai.app/pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/pipelines/)** lists them next to the pipelines the community shares, each with what it saved and how that was measured. Installing one is a single command: ```bash rtk pipeline add github:user/repo # check and install a shared pipeline ``` A pipeline can rewrite commands and send content to the models it declares, so read its file before you install it. Written once, a pipeline works in every agent RTK supports, as far as that agent's hooks allow: **[Agent Coverage](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/agent-coverage/)** shows what runs where. > Start here: **[Pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/overview/)** · the built-ins, explained: **[Reference Pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/reference-pipelines/)** · write and share your own: **[Writing a Pipeline](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/writing-pipelines/)**, **[Pipeline Commands](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/commands/)** ### RTK Proxy (optional) The `rtk-proxy` daemon runs the same pipeline on your agent's **provider-API traffic**: it strips bytes no model ever needed without breaking the prompt cache, and carries the calls your pipeline routes to cheaper models on the credential your agent already sends, so they show up in `rtk gain
manifest_content:
# Two crates, one binary. `rtk` (Apache-2.0) is the CLI; `engine` (BUSL-1.1)
# is `rtk-engine`, the pure compression core the CLI LINKS -- so the shipped
# `rtk` binary contains BUSL-1.1 code, and engine/LICENSE carries an
# Additional Use Grant covering production use as part of that binary.
#
# `proxy/` is DELIBERATELY NOT a member, but note what that does and does
# not buy: cargo scans every manifest in the repository regardless of
# membership, so a bare `cargo install --git <url>` still aborts with
# "multiple packages with binaries found" as long as proxy/ declares a
# [[bin]]. Non-membership only keeps tokio/axum out of the CLI's dependency
# graph and lockfile. The documented install command therefore names the
# package (`cargo install --git <url> rtk`), and the daemon is built
# explicitly from its own directory:
#   cargo build --release --manifest-path proxy/Cargo.toml
#
# The cost of the split is that `libsqlite3-sys` (which declares
# `links = "sqlite3"`) is pinned by hand in both lockfiles: rusqlite 0.34 here
# and in proxy/Cargo.toml, matching what icm-store links. Do not bump one
# alone. CI lints and tests the daemon in its own job.
[workspace]
members = [".", "text", "engine", "plugin"]

[package]
name = "rtk"
version = "0.49.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.91"
authors = ["RTK AI Labs"]
description = "Rust Token Killer - High-performance CLI proxy to minimize LLM token consumption"
license = "Apache-2.0"
homepage = "https://www.rtk-ai.app"
repository = "https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk"
readme = "README.md"
keywords = ["cli", "llm", "token", "filter", "productivity"]
categories = ["command-line-utilities", "development-tools"]

[lib]
# The lib target exists so a plugin host can call `rtk::entry()`. rtk is an
# application, not a library API: every module here is private, so a doctest —
# which compiles as an external crate and sees only `pub` items — can never
# reach them. Running doctests would test the examples against themselves.
doctest = false

[features]
# The full edition. `--no-default-features` builds the Apache-2.0 hook core
# alone: no rtk-engine in the dependency graph, no BUSL code in the binary.
default = ["engine"]
engine = ["dep:rtk-engine"]
example-plugins = ["engine", "dep:rtk-plugin"]

[dependencies]
rtk-engine = { path = "engine", optional = true }
rtk-plugin = { path = "plugin", optional = true }
rtk-text = { path = "text" }
clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }
anyhow = "1.0"
# Console code page decoding for child-process output. Kept off the
# cfg(windows) target so the mapping and the incremental UTF-8 walk stay
# compiled — and unit-tested — on every platform; only the code page *lookup*
# is Windows-specific. codepage covers the ANSI/DBCS pages encoding_rs
# implements, oem_cp the legacy OEM/DOS pages (437, 850, …) it does not.
encoding_rs = "0.8"
codepage = "0.1"
oem_cp = "2"
ignore = "0.4"
walkdir = "2"
regex = "1"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = { version = "1", features = ["preserve_order"] }
colored = "3"
dirs = "7"
# Pinned to what the proxy crate's icm-store links: libsqlite3-sys declares
# `links = "sqlite3"`, and two versions of it cannot coexist in one workspace
# resolve. See proxy/Cargo.toml.
rusqlite = { version = "0.42", features = ["bundled"] }
toml = "1.2"
toml_edit = "0.22"
chrono = "0.4"
tempfile = "3"
sha2 = "0.11"
base16ct = "1"
ureq = { version = "3", features = ["json"] }
getrandom = "0.4"
flate2 = "1.0"
quick-xml = "0.42"
which = "8"
# `rtk gain --watch`: a live full-screen dashboard over the same two SQLite
# sources the static view reads (core::tracking + the llm-proxy's own DB).
# Opt-in, not on the hot startup path -- doesn't affect the <10ms budget.
ratatui = "0.30"
crossterm = "0.29"

[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]
libc = "0.2"

[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]
windows-sys = { version = "0.61", features = [
    "Win32_System_Console",
    "Win32_Globalization",
] }

# musl's built-in malloc makes ~1,700 mmap/munmap calls and ~8,000 extra page
# faults per `rtk hook claude`, more than twice the CPU of a glibc build. Use
# mimalloc on musl targets only; glibc, macOS and Windows builds are unchanged.
# `no_thp` skips mimalloc's madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) on its arena: with transparent
# huge pages set to `madvise` (the Ubuntu default) it makes the first page faults
# stall in memory compaction, up to 100+ ms per call on a fragmented host.
[target.'cfg(target_env = "musl")'.dependencies]
mimalloc = { version = "0.1", features = ["no_thp"] }

[build-dependencies]
toml = "1.2"

[dev-dependencies]
# Safe, closure-scoped env mutation for tests. std::env::set_var is unsafe
# in edition 2024 and has no safe std replacement; temp-env restores the
# previous value on completion or panic and serializes callers internally.
temp-env = "0.3"

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = true
codegen-units = 1
# NOT `panic = "abort"`. `hooks::posthook::run` wraps the whole method chain in
# `catch_unwind` as th

readme_content:
---

--- Enable Claude Code, Codex, or any agent to use your real phone. The agent can scroll, tap, type, and read your phone with no jailbreak, no Xcode, and nothing installed on the phone. > **iPhone** through the Mac's iPhone Mirroring window
> **Android** over adb from macOS, Linux or Windows
> **Phone Harness Cloud** phone: an Android over adb, or an iPhone over HTTPS ``` ● agent: wants to open Weather │ ● find_text("Weather") → (400, 468) │ ● tap(400, 468) → reads the screen → forecast is up ✓ done ``` Try [Phone Harness Cloud](https://phone-harness.com/dashboard?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=cloud) → Hosted iPhones and Androids with stealth, real numbers, 2FA, and unlimited devices Get started by sending the [setup prompt](https://phone-harness.com?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=setup-prompt) to your coding agent. ## Demo **Task:** "Buy me a Waymo to Delah Coffee from my current location." ## Setup For the CLI, send this setup prompt to your agent (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Bot, and more): ```text Install or upgrade phone-harness to the latest stable version with uv using Python 3.12, register the skill from `phone-harness skill`, then read https://github.com/phone-harness/phone-harness/blob/main/onboarding.md and walk me through it. Follow https://github.com/phone-harness/phone-harness/blob/main/install.md if setup or connection fails. ``` The agent installs the CLI, asks which phone to use, and walks you through the steps that need your hands. What each phone needs: | Phone | Needs | | --- | --- | | **iPhone** | macOS 15+, iPhone Mirroring paired to an iOS 18+ iPhone, Accessibility and Screen Recording permission | | **Android** | adb and USB debugging, on macOS, Linux or Windows | | **Cloud Android / iPhone** | [Phone Harness Cloud](https://phone-harness.com/dashboard?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=setup-table) account; cloud Android also needs adb | `phone-harness doctor` checks the setup. Full details: [install.md](install.md) and [setup/](setup/). **MCP:** add `https://mcp.phone-harness.com/mcp` to any MCP client ([setup](https://github.com/phone-harness/mcp)). Cloud Android and iPhone only for now. **Hermes Agent:** `hermes plugins install phone-harness/phone-harness/integrations/hermes`. See [integrations/hermes](integrations/hermes/README.md). **OpenClaw:** `openclaw plugins install clawhub:phone-harness`. See [integrations/openclaw](integrations/openclaw/README.md). ## Usage ```bash phone-harness <<'PY' open_app("Notes") tap_text("New Note") type_text("hello from the harness") print([o["text"] for o in screen()][:10]) PY ``` Helpers are pre-imported; [helpers.py](src/phone_harness/helpers.py) has the full list. The agent saves its own helpers in `~/.phone-harness/agent-workspace`. ## Phone Harness Cloud No phone on your desk, or need more than one? [Phone Harness Cloud](https://phone-harness.com/dashboard?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=cloud-section) hosts them for you: - **Android phones** on demand: a fresh one per session, or a saved phone that keeps its apps and logins. - **Dedicated real iPhones**, driven over HTTPS from any OS. - **A live view** of the phone in your browser while the agent works. ```bash phone-harness cloud login # once: approve in your browser phone-harness cloud ls # phones on the account, and any live session phone-harness cloud start # cloud.phone if set, else a temporary Android; 15 min (--for 90s, 15m) phone-harness cloud start ios # the account's iPhone, when only one is listed phone-harness <<'PY' print(screenshot()) PY phone-harness cloud stop # ends the session; a saved Android is written back ``` The same helpers drive a cloud phone: an Android over adb, an iPhone over HTTPS. `cloud start` takes a phone's name or id from `cloud ls`, or `ios` / `android`; with none it starts a temporary Android. `phone-harness cloud` lists every command. No cloud iPhone on the account yet, or need more of them? Reserve them with a $20 per phone refundable deposit. The command prints a quote, which is the authoritative figure, and a Stripe Checkout link. You pay in your browser, and that payment is what holds your place in the queue, which is in the order deposits were paid; the CLI never pays for you. ```bash phone-harness cloud reserve --type iphone --plan monthly --qty 2 \ --use-case "Testing our app on real iPhones" --open phone-harness cloud reservations # status, place in the queue, deposit, when it was paid phone-harness cloud reservations cancel ID # leave the queue; the deposit still held goes back to the card that paid ``` `--type` is `iphone` or `iphone-esim`, and `--plan` is `monthly` or `annual`. Reservations are for iPhones only (with or without eSIM). Cloud Android emulators are on the $20 plan and are not reserved. The plan starts when a phone is handed over; the deposit comes off its first bill and is then no longer refundable. An account can have five unpaid reservations an hour, and cancelling one does not free a place. ## How it works Every phone sits behind the same helpers, so a script written for one runs on the others. - **iPhone:** captures the iPhone Mirroring window, reads it with Apple's Vision OCR, and sends taps, swipes and typing as input events. - **Android:** adb for screenshots and input, the accessibility tree for text. USB or Wi-Fi. - **Cloud Android:** the same as Android, over adb to a hosted phone. - **Cloud iPhone:** ops over HTTPS. `phone-harness config set platform ios|android` picks the default phone. `phone-harness update` upgrades the CLI, and it prints one line when a new version is out (`PHONE_HARNESS_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` silences it). ## Limits - Unlocking the iPhone pauses mirroring; a PIN-locked Android needs the user. - OCR sees text, not icons. Unlabeled controls need a screenshot and a vision-capable model. - No multi-touch, no camera or Face ID flows. DRM video renders black. - Connecting the phone is always the user's job. ## Sponsor phone-harness is free and maintained in my own time. [Sponsoring](https://github.com/sponsors/ShawnPana) keeps it that way.

[project]
name = "phone-harness"
version = "0.3.3"
description = "Let an agent drive a real phone: an iPhone through macOS iPhone Mirroring, an Android over adb, a rented cloud Android, or a cloud iPhone over HTTPS"
readme = "README.md"
license = "MIT"
license-files = ["LICENSE"]
requires-python = ">=3.10"
keywords = ["iphone", "android", "adb", "automation", "agent", "iphone-mirroring", "cloud-phone"]
classifiers = [
    "Development Status :: 3 - Alpha",
    "Environment :: Console",
    "Operating System :: MacOS",
    "Operating System :: POSIX :: Linux",
    "Operating System :: Microsoft :: Windows",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
    "Topic :: Software Development :: Testing",
]
dependencies = [
    # iPhone control (iPhone Mirroring, Vision OCR) needs macOS. Android is
    # plain adb and installs everywhere; these are skipped off macOS.
    "pyobjc-framework-Quartz; sys_platform == 'darwin'",
    "pyobjc-framework-Vision; sys_platform == 'darwin'",
    "pyobjc-framework-Cocoa; sys_platform == 'darwin'",
    "pyobjc-framework-ApplicationServices; sys_platform == 'darwin'",
]

[project.urls]
Homepage = "https://phone-harness.com"
Repository = "https://github.com/phone-harness/phone-harness"
Documentation = "https://phone-harness.com/docs"
Issues = "https://github.com/phone-harness/phone-harness/issues"

[project.scripts]
phone-harness = "phone_harness.run:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/phone_harness"]

# Shipped inside the package so an install works without a checkout.
# agent-workspace/ stays the only copy in the repo; the wheel maps its
# default file to phone_harness/agent_workspace/. Only that file is
# packed: a .env or scratch file beside it must never ride along.
[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]
"SKILL.md" = "phone_harness/SKILL.md"
"agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py" = "phone_harness/agent_workspace/agent_helpers.py"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.sdist]
include = ["src/phone_harness", "SKILL.md", "onboarding.md", "README.md", "LICENSE", "install.md", "setup", "agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py"]

name: LoopForge
description: Self-hosted workflows for coding-agent delivery. Orchestrate CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code with scripts and human approval gates. Includes Local workflows for coding assistants.
readme_content:
English · 简体中文

Two ways to work · Quick start · SOPs · Features · Local (Legacy) · FAQ · Docs

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8af401d9-1aae-427c-b4bc-455c12d17beb

80-second product tour (1080p, with sound).

**LoopForge** is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to **Main Bot** in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as an **SOP** (a standard workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in. Coding-agent CLIs do the work: CodeBuddy, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Pi, DeepSeek Harness and ZCode. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license. ## Two ways to work | | **Chat with Main Bot** | **Run an SOP** | | --- | --- | --- | | Best for | Exploring, quick fixes, iterating with the agent | Repeatable delivery with fixed stages and sign-off | | How it runs | Main Bot opens a [conversation workspace](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) (a Docker sandbox with your repos) on demand and calls project roles as subagents | The engine runs Agent, Script, Human-gate and sub-SOP nodes in order, in their own sandbox | | You stay in control by | Queuing or steering messages mid-reply, and pausing, resuming or taking over a running SOP from chat | Approving at human gates, sending work back to a chosen step, retrying or rerunning from any node | | Delivers | A PR/MR, or a direct merge into a shared branch (`mode=direct`) | Documents, code or a PR, plus per-node artifacts and logs | Both paths track the same **requirements**, so every change, whether made in chat or by an SOP, links back to what was asked for and counts toward delivery and cost reports.

The chat home. Type a request, @ a role, skill, requirement, SOP or repository, and pick the executor, model and permission mode per conversation.

## Why LoopForge Ask a coding agent to "fix this bug" and the result depends on that run. It might skip the plan, forget the tests, review its own code, or stop halfway without anyone noticing. That's fine for a demo, but it isn't how a team ships. - **Repeatable.** Same SOP, same stages, same checks for every requirement. Start from built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs. - **Separated roles.** Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools. A role works as an SOP node or as a subagent in chat. - **Human on the loop.** Agents run on their own while you supervise. Pause, steer or take over anytime, and approval gates stop the run where a human must decide: approve, or send the work back to a chosen step. - **Observable and resumable.** Node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts in one place. Pause, retry a failed step, or rerun from any node. - **Your stack, your servers.** Ten coding-agent CLIs as executors, from CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code to OpenCode, Cursor CLI and more. GitHub, Skills and MCP as tools. Docker sandboxes or your own machine as the runtime. ## Quick start Install **Git** and clone the repository first. The installer checks Docker, Compose, Python 3 and curl and offers to install missing components. Python/curl installation supports apt, dnf and yum on Linux; the Compose plugin supports x86_64/arm64 and verifies the official release SHA-256. macOS needs a working Python 3 and Docker Desktop; Homebrew can install missing components. Ordinary Linux users are supported through Docker group access or sudo. Set `LOOPFORGE_YES=1` to accept installation prompts. Package and image downloads require internet access. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git cd LoopForge ./start.sh ``` `./start.sh` pulls the GHCR release image pinned in `compose.yaml` without building locally (`bash scripts/install.sh` does the same). It creates the MySQL and platform services, generates configuration and session secrets, and installs the built-in sandboxes, starter SOPs and welcome project. Host Go and Node.js installations are not required. Configure model API keys and GitHub authorization after startup. Use `./start.sh logs`, `stop`, `restart` or `pull` to manage it, and `./start.sh dev` to build the checkout from source. If downloads from `ghcr.io` stall, `./start.sh` and `./start.sh pull` time `ghcr.io` against the Nanjing University mirror [ghcr.nju.edu.cn](https://doc.nju.edu.cn/books/e1654/page/ghcr). Nanjing is used only when its manifest digest matches the digest just read from ghcr.io; the script pulls that digest and tags it back to the name pinned in `compose.yaml`, which trusts that host because the result is tagged with the official name. A missing official digest, a mismatch, or a failed mirror pull stays on `ghcr.io`. `MIRROR=ghcr.io` forces the upstream registry and `MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn` forces Nanjing; the choice is not written to `.env`. The GitHub Release records the digest; `docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge:` should show the same digest after `@`. `compose.yaml` stays unchanged. A Docker `registry-mirrors` entry such as `https://docker.nju.edu.cn` only accelerates Docker Hub and is not a value for `MIRROR`. ```bash ./start.sh MIRROR=ghcr.io ./start.sh MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn ./start.sh pull ``` Open the address printed by the installer and create your account; the first one becomes the administrator. The service listens on `0.0.0.0:8090` by default. On a cloud host, the installer reads the public IP from the provider's metadata service and prints it; allow the port in your security group, or put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front. Restrict access to your own IP until the administrator account exists. The home page's quick-access guide walks you through adding a model key, connecting a repository and choosing an SOP. For GitLab, Gitea, Gogs and other Git hosts, [set up Git SSH](docs/deployment.md#git-repositories-over-ssh) to check out and push branches with a personal key. PR/MR and Issue automation requires a hosting API token or a separately configured MCP. ### Try it without an API key New accounts join the **LoopForge demo project**, which includes an SOP made only of a script and a human gate: 1. Switch to the demo project, open **Templates**, and open **Platform check · script & approval**. 2. Click **Run SOP**. A real script writes a report, then the run waits for you at the approval step. 3. Approve it from **Needs review** or the run page, and watch the run continue to its final artifact. ### What you need for real work | I want to… | You need | | --- | --- | | Run the script + approval demo | Nothing | | Chat with Main Bot, generate a document or a new project | An API key for the selected executor | | Change an existing repository (in chat or via an SOP) and open a PR | Model credentials and a GitHub repository (connect GitHub in personal settings) |
More setup details: executors, GitHub, sandboxes, access model
- **Executors.** Choose a CLI and model for chat, requirement clarification, Bot replies, notification reports, run evaluation, or static preview. Each SOP role can select its own CLI, and built-in templates still default to CodeBuddy. Scheduled prompts use the CLI selected on the schedule. The platform can run without a CodeBuddy installation or key once its workflows use other CLIs. [Deployment and upgrade](docs/deployment.md#choosing-an-executor) | Executor | Credentials | Installation | | --- | --- | --- | | **CodeBuddy** | Personal key, or a shared key an administrator configures for chat and SOP runs | Bundled by default, optional on source builds | | **Codex** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | In the Docker image | | **Claude Code** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **OpenCode · Kimi Code · Pi** | Personal key only | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **DeepSeek Harness** | Personal key only | In the Docker image | | **Cursor CLI** | Personal key only | Provider installer on first chat use; not installed into SOP sandboxes | | **Antigravity** | Personal key, or the connected execution machine owner's existing account login | Install the official CLI on the execution machine and in Docker images used for SOP runs | | **ZCode** | Personal key only | Not bundled; install it on the service or execution machine PATH | The seven agent CLIs after Claude Code keep their model and MCP configuration in a private home directory per run. Antigravity can reuse the execution machine owner's account login in conversation workspaces and native or Docker SOP sandboxes. Its official CLI refreshes the credential copy, and the Runner saves the refreshed login back to its original local store. Gemini API keys use separate API billing. The other agent CLIs use the responsible user's own key and Base URL from personal settings, including on a connected execution machine. First-use installs need npm or provider access; [native deployments](docs/deployment.md#workers-and-runners) need the CLI for the executor you choose. - **WeCom notifications.** The image built from this Dockerfile includes `wecom-cli`; published images gain it with the next release. Native installations need to install it separately; see [Deployment](docs/deployment.md#native-development). - **GitHub is optional.** All built-in generic SOPs run without a repository: product SOPs deliver documents, and new frontend/backend projects deliver source files in the task workspace. Bug fixes still

name: OpenSpec
description: Spec-driven development (SDD) for AI coding assistants.
readme_content:
The most loved spec framework. [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/Fission-AI/OpenSpec?style=flat-square&label=Stars)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/stargazers) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/@fission-ai/openspec?style=flat-square&label=Downloads/mo)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@fission-ai/openspec) [![Contributors](https://img.shields.io/github/contributors/Fission-AI/OpenSpec?style=flat-square&label=Contributors)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/graphs/contributors)

Our philosophy: ```text → fluid not rigid → iterative not waterfall → easy not complex → built for brownfield not just greenfield → scalable from personal projects to enterprises ```

Follow @0xTab on X for updates · Join the OpenSpec Discord for help and questions.

## See it in action ```text You: /openspec-explore AI: What would you like to explore? You: I want dark mode but I'm not sure how to do it cleanly. AI: Let me look at your styling setup... Cleanest path here: CSS variables + a small theme context, with system-preference detection. No new dependencies. Scope it? You: Yes, let's do it. You: /openspec-propose add-dark-mode AI: Created openspec/changes/add-dark-mode/ ✓ proposal.md — why we're doing this, what's changing ✓ specs/ — requirements and scenarios ✓ design.md — technical approach ✓ tasks.md — implementation checklist Ready for implementation! You: /openspec-apply-change AI: Implementing tasks... ✓ 1.1 Add theme context provider ✓ 1.2 Create toggle component ✓ 2.1 Add CSS variables ✓ 2.2 Wire up localStorage All tasks complete! You: /openspec-archive-change AI: Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/ Specs updated. Ready for the next feature. ```
What do the specs actually look like? Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the `specs/` folder created above: ```markdown ## ADDED Requirements ### Requirement: Theme selection The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes, defaulting to the system preference. #### Scenario: User toggles dark mode - **WHEN** the user clicks the theme toggle - **THEN** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice ``` Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written. OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live [specs](openspec/specs) and in-flight [changes](openspec/changes) for real examples at scale.
OpenSpec Dashboard

## Why teams adopt OpenSpec Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists. **[Stores](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores)** are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same `openspec/` shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by `git push` like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo. - **Cross-repo features** — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos. - **Shared requirements** — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki. - **Plan before code** — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later. > Stores are in **beta**. Start with the [Stores guide](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores). ## Quick Start Install OpenSpec. On macOS or Linux, in your terminal: ```bash curl -fsSL https://openspec.dev/cli/install.sh | sh ``` On Windows, in PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://openspec.dev/cli/install.ps1 | iex ``` Prefer a package manager? `npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest` (needs Node.js 22.20.0 or higher) or the official [Homebrew formula](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/openspec), `brew install openspec`. Then navigate to your project directory and initialize: ```bash cd your-project openspec init ``` > **Want your AI to do it?** Paste the [setup prompt](https://openspec.dev/docs/installation#install-with-your-ai-assistant) into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs `openspec init`, and verifies the result. Now talk to your AI: - **Not sure what to build yet?** Start with `/openspec-explore`, a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. ([Quickstart](https://openspec.dev/docs/quickstart)) - **Already know what you want?** Go straight to `/openspec-propose `. Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow (`openspec-new-change`, `openspec-continue-change`, `openspec-ff-change`, `openspec-verify-change`, `openspec-bulk-archive-change`, `openspec-onboard`), select it with `openspec config profile` and apply with `openspec update`. These are skills. Most tools invoke them as `/openspec-propose` and Codex as `$openspec-propose`, or you can ask for the work in plain words. `openspec init` prints the right form for the tools you picked — see [Supported Tools](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools). Coming from 1.x and its `/opsx:*` commands? See [Upgrade to 2.0](https://openspec.dev/docs/upgrade-to-2). > [!NOTE] > Not sure if your tool is supported? [View the full list](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools) – we support 30+ tools and growing. > > Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. [See installation options](https://openspec.dev/docs/installation). ## Docs Full documentation lives at **[openspec.dev/docs](https://openspec.dev/docs)**. → **[Quickstart](https://openspec.dev/docs/quickstart)**: your first change, start to finish
→ **[Set up your project](https://openspec.dev/docs/setup)**: what `openspec init` installs
→ **[CLI](https://openspec.dev/docs/cli)**: terminal reference
→ **[Supported Tools](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools)**: tool integrations & install paths
→ **[Customize](https://openspec.dev/docs/customize)**: profiles, project config, and schemas
→ **[Stores](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores)**: plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta)
→ **[Community Showcase](docs/community.md)**: projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec ## Community schemas Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how [github/spec-kit's community extension catalog](https://github.com/github/spec-kit/tree/main/extensions) handles tool integrations. → **[Browse the catalog](docs/customization.md#community-schemas)** in the customization docs. ## Why OpenSpec? AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written. - **Agree before you build** — human and AI align on specs before code gets written - **Stay organized** — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks - **Work fluidly** — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates - **Use your tools** — works with 30+ AI assistants via skills ### How we compare **vs. [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit)** (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely. **vs. [Kiro](https://kiro.dev)** (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use. **vs. nothing** — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony. ## Updating OpenSpec **Upgrade the CLI** With the standalone install, run `openspec install`. If you installed with npm: ```bash npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest ``` If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew: ```bash brew upgrade openspec ``` **Refresh agent instructions** Run this once to refresh the skills installed on your machine. If your team keeps skills in Git, run it in each project that commits them. ```bash openspec update ``` ## Usage Notes **Model selection**: OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation. **Context hygiene**: OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session. ## Contributing Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us. → **[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)**: the full process, from first issue to merged PR ## Other
Telemetry OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats. We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI. **Opt-out (any one is enough):** - `openspec config set telemetry.enabled false` (global config; unset means on) - `export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0` or `export DO_NOT_TRACK=1` (env overrides config)
Maintainers & Advisors See [MAINTAINERS.md](MAINTAINERS.md) for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project.
## License MIT

[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = ["src-tauri", "crates/dbx-core", "crates/dbx-driver-agent", "crates/dbx-driver-support", "crates/dbx-driver-elasticsearch", "crates/dbx-driver-mongodb", "crates/dbx-driver-mysql", "crates/dbx-driver-postgres", "crates/dbx-driver-redis", "crates/dbx-driver-sqlserver", "crates/dbx-drivers", "crates/dbx-sql", "crates/dbx-sql-core", "crates/dbx-sql-data", "crates/dbx-sql-dialect", "crates/dbx-sql-schema", "crates/dbx-plugin-runtime", "crates/dbx-formats", "crates/dbx-types", "crates/dbx-platform", "crates/dbx-ai-provider", "crates/dbx-web", "crates/dbx-mcp", "crates/dbx-cli", "crates/dbx-sqlite-worker", "crates/dbx-tauri-consul", "crates/dbx-tauri-schema"]
exclude = ["vendor/tauri-plugin-updater", "vendor/tauri-plugin-single-instance", "vendor/ctor", "vendor/dirs-sys", "vendor/pageant", "vendor/rumqttc", "vendor/tiberius", "vendor/webview2-com-sys", "vendor/wry"]

[patch.crates-io]
tauri-plugin-single-instance = { path = "vendor/tauri-plugin-single-instance" }
# The offline Win7 / Server 2012 R2 bundle links the WebView2 SDK 1.0.902.49
# loader. Loaders >= 1.0.1054.31 import EventSetInformation, which Win7 and
# Server 2012 R2 do not provide. Keep that loader in the source tree instead of
# swapping a file inside the cargo registry, because a registry swap bypasses
# compile caches and once shipped a binary linked against the wrong loader.
webview2-com-sys = { path = "vendor/webview2-com-sys" }
# Offline signed update restoration and checked Windows installer launch.
tauri-plugin-updater = { path = "vendor/tauri-plugin-updater" }
# Tauri 2.11 uses ctor 0.8, which excludes Rust's win7 vendor. This vendors
# upstream rust-ctor#443 until tauri-utils moves to ctor 1.x.
ctor = { path = "vendor/ctor" }
# rumqttc 0.24 hardcodes MQTT 3.1.1; this patch adds MQTT 3.1 CONNECT encoding.
rumqttc = { path = "vendor/rumqttc" }
# Keep two small upstream crates on Win7-compatible API calls. Their current
# Windows bindings otherwise import COMBASE or WinRT APIs unavailable on Win7.
dirs-sys = { path = "vendor/dirs-sys" }
pageant = { path = "vendor/pageant" }
# Wry 0.55 probes and creates WebView2 with a null browser folder. Pass the
# bundled Fixed Runtime path explicitly so Windows 7 does not fall back to an
# unavailable system Runtime. The vendored copy also intercepts the WebView2
# F6 "Focus Next Pane" accelerator to prevent a black screen on frameless
# Overlay-titlebar windows, and registers a ProcessFailed handler that
# auto-recovers the webview when the renderer process fails while the host
# process stays alive (black screen after an overnight idle session, see
# vendor/wry/src/webview2/mod.rs). Recovery is layered by process kind
# (browser exit is fatal, GPU exits are self-healed by WebView2) and bounded
# by a cooldown plus a maximum reload budget. It also re-owns clipboard
# writes performed by the WebView2 browser process on the host window so
# copies show up in Windows Clipboard History / Win+V
# (MicrosoftEdge/WebView2Feedback#5650, see
# vendor/wry/src/webview2/clipboard_history.rs).
wry = { path = "vendor/wry" }
tokio-postgres = { git = "https://github.com/t8y2/tokio-postgres-gaussdb.git", rev = "5f37ebd1ae8e2c81ac07b89a046c9319f7a1bc89" }
postgres-types = { git = "https://github.com/t8y2/tokio-postgres-gaussdb.git", rev = "5f37ebd1ae8e2c81ac07b89a046c9319f7a1bc89" }
postgres-protocol = { git = "https://github.com/t8y2/tokio-postgres-gaussdb.git", rev = "5f37ebd1ae8e2c81ac07b89a046c9319f7a1bc89" }
# Temporary compatibility patches for deprecated sha256_password accounts and
# rustls dangerous-mode connections to legacy certificates. Remove after upstream support lands.
mysql_async = { git = "https://github.com/t8y2/mysql_async.git", rev = "4cd84d86bb86b060320ce3459561e8093e4422fa" }
# Preserve readable SQL Server result sets when a row contains an unpaired
# UTF-16 surrogate, or varchar/text bytes that are invalid in the column's
# collation (replaced with U+FFFD, no BOM sniffing). Remove after the behavior
# is available in upstream tiberius.
tiberius = { path = "vendor/tiberius" }

[profile.dev.package."*"]
# Dependencies are never breakpoint-inspected in dev; line tables keep
# backtraces resolvable while shrinking dev/test build time and artifacts.
debug = "line-tables-only"

[profile.release]
panic = "abort"
strip = true
lto = true
codegen-units = 1
opt-level = "s"

name: FreeVideo
description: Make videos on the computer you already own. FreeVideo runs MiniMax H3 in as little as 8 GB of VRAM and 16 GB of RAM, and adapts its acceleration path to your hardware.
readme_content:
| Windows | macOS | Linux | Community Results | Gallery | Discord | QQ Group | WeChat Group |

English · 中文

Make videos on the computer you already own. Powered by [Video DeltaNet (VDN)](https://openvdn.github.io/), FreeVideo runs MiniMax H3 in as little as 8 GB of VRAM and 16 GB of RAM on NVIDIA graphics cards with compute capability 8.0 or higher (such as the RTX 30 series or newer, professional cards included), with acceleration adapted to your hardware. Apple silicon Macs run a preview. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ecda7d0d-7fbe-4e0c-8c29-8f3315bafc15

More clips and the four quality levels side by side in the gallery →

## News - **2026-11-10** · **[v0.5.0](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/tag/v0.5.0): H3 Image.** Pictures up to 16 MP locally, from 8 GB of VRAM. - **2026-10-13** · **[v0.4.0](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/tag/v0.4.0): AI agents, minute-long videos and an editing view.** Let an AI agent such as Claude Code or Codex make videos on its own, generate videos over a minute long, and edit them on a timeline. - **2026-10-07** · **[v0.3.2](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/tag/v0.3.2): preview first.** See a half-resolution preview first and finish only the videos you like. - **2026-10-07** · **[v0.3.0](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/tag/v0.3.0): a faster int8 model.** GeForce and RTX 30-series cards switch to int8; an RTX 3090 makes a 5-second video about 2.3x faster. - **2026-10-06** · **[Gallery](https://freevideo-community.pages.dev/#gallery) is live.** Watch 20-second clips made with FreeVideo, and the four quality levels side by side. - **2026-10-06** · **[v0.2.3](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/tag/v0.2.3): videos carry their workflow.** Drop a FreeVideo video onto the ComfyUI canvas to restore its prompt, seed and settings. Earlier videos can get theirs too. - **2026-10-05** · **[v0.2.0](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/tag/v0.2.0): four quality levels.** Choose Light, Medium, High or Max for each video; higher levels give higher quality but take longer. Results can be exported as sharing images or videos with the generation time and GPU. - **2026-10-05** · **[v0.1.2](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/tag/v0.1.2): FreeVideo on Mac.** Apple silicon Macs generate MiniMax H3 videos locally (preview). - **2026-10-03** · **Community LoRAs.** Use MiniMax H3 LoRAs right in your workflow. See [examples](docs/LoRA.md). - **2026-10-02** · **FreeVideo is open source.** MiniMax H3 on consumer GPUs with as little as 8 GB of VRAM. ## About FreeVideo is a local inference engine for MiniMax H3 on consumer GPUs, built on [OpenVDN](https://github.com/OpenVDN)'s 8-step [VDN-H3](https://huggingface.co/OpenVDN/vdn-minimax-h3) model with [Video DeltaNet](https://openvdn.github.io/)'s hybrid attention. It coordinates VRAM, system memory and disk, adapting weight placement, compute precision and attention kernels to the available hardware. FreeVideo runs as a ComfyUI plugin, with launchers for Windows, macOS and Linux. Its core features include: - **Hardware-adaptive execution**: Chooses the weight format for each GPU, int8 on GeForce RTX 30, 40 and 50 series cards and other Ampere cards, and FP8 on workstation and datacenter cards of newer architectures, and automatically probes the available attention kernels. - **Low-memory inference**: Weight streaming, asynchronous prefetching and chunked computation keep peak memory low, enabling inference with as little as 8 GB of VRAM and 16 GB of RAM. - **Multimodal inputs**: Text prompts, first and last frames, and image, video and audio references. - **Community LoRAs**: Use MiniMax H3 LoRAs in your workflow. See [examples](docs/LoRA.md). - **ComfyUI integration**: A dedicated creative workspace inside ComfyUI that supports two-pass sampling and batch generation and keeps a history of past creations. For finer control, switch to the node view to add LoRAs or customize the workflow. - **One-click deployment**: The Windows, Mac and Linux launchers set up ComfyUI, the runtime environment and the models, reuse existing models, and support offline installation. ## Getting Started ### Windows 1. [Download FreeVideo.exe](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/latest/download/FreeVideo.exe) and run it. 2. Select an existing ComfyUI folder or install a new one. Existing model folders can be added for reuse; missing models are downloaded automatically. 3. Click **Install & launch**. ComfyUI opens in the browser with the FreeVideo workspace.
**Security software:** FreeVideo.exe is code-signed. If security software blocks FreeVideo.exe or quarantines files in the FreeVideo folder, check that the SHA-256 of FreeVideo.exe matches the value on the release page, then restore the files and add the FreeVideo folder to the software's exclusion list. **Offline installation:** Download the packages from [Quark](https://pan.quark.cn/s/c51235b84618) and drag the ZIP files into the launcher without extracting them. A fully offline installation needs the four model packs (video model, text encoder, video & audio decoder, and sampling caches), plus the environment package for a new ComfyUI installation. After importing only the environment package, you can also choose **Automatic download** for the models (v0.3.12 or newer). The audio reference cache is optional and is used only when a reference includes audio. ### macOS (Apple silicon preview) 1. [Download FreeVideo-Mac-arm64.dmg](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/latest/download/FreeVideo-Mac-arm64.dmg), open it and drag **FreeVideo.app** into **Applications**. 2. Open FreeVideo, then select an existing ComfyUI folder or install a new one. Existing model folders can be added for reuse; the runtime environment and missing models are downloaded automatically. 3. Click **Install & launch**. ComfyUI opens in the browser with the FreeVideo workspace. This preview has been tested on an M5 Mac with 24 GB of unified memory. See the [Mac guide](docs/Mac.md) for generation times and memory. The Mac preview isn't notarized by Apple yet, so macOS blocks it the first time you open it. Download it only from the Releases page, then check the file and approve it as described in the [Mac guide](docs/Mac.md#first-open). This approves FreeVideo only; your other security settings stay as they are. ### Existing ComfyUI Install FreeVideo as a custom node: ```bash cd ComfyUI/custom_nodes git clone https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo.git ``` Restart ComfyUI, open **Workflow → Browse Templates → FreeVideo → FreeVideo-All-in-One**, and complete the setup in FreeVideo **Settings**. To update, run `git pull` in `custom_nodes/FreeVideo` (or update the node in ComfyUI-Manager) and restart ComfyUI. ### Linux **Desktop:** [Download FreeVideo-Linux-x86_64.AppImage](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/releases/latest/download/FreeVideo-Linux-x86_64.AppImage), make it executable and open it, then follow the same steps as on Windows. **Terminal or server:** ```bash git clone https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo.git && cd FreeVideo ./setup.sh ``` Setup installs FreeVideo, ComfyUI and the models, then opens FreeVideo in the browser. Afterwards, type `freevideo` to open it again. On a server, connect from your own computer through SSH, or run `freevideo server --listen 0.0.0.0` for an access link on your local network. See the [Linux guide](docs/Linux.md). ### More details - [FreeVideo Adaptive Execution Planner](docs/execution-planning.md) - [Community results](docs/community-results.md) - [Thanks to the community](docs/community-thanks.md) ### Support Report bugs in [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo/issues), or ask questions on [Discord](https://discord.gg/MsA277cJzZ), [QQ](https://freevideo-community.pages.dev/qq) or [WeChat](https://freevideo-community.pages.dev/wechat). ## Citation FreeVideo is based on VDN-H3. If you use FreeVideo in your research, please cite the [Video DeltaNet paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20744): ```bibtex @article{xi2026videodeltanet, title={Video DeltaNet: A Video-Native Hybrid Attention for Livestream Video Generation}, author={Xi, Haocheng and Xie, Yiming and Zhao, Hexu and Zhang, Yiwen and Liu, Michael and Creavin, Thomas and Keutzer, Kurt and Li, Xiuyu and Lv, Zhaoyang and Xu, Chenfeng and Feng, Haiwen}, journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.20744}, year={2026} } ``` ## Team ### Project Team [Bowen Xue](https://github.com/KBRASK) · [Shuo Yang](https://github.com/andy-yang-1) · [Haocheng Xi](https://github.com/haochengxi) · [Xiaoze Fan](https://github.com/jason-fxz) · [Chenfeng Xu](https://github.com/chenfengxu714) ### Special Thanks Special thanks to [**AIwood爱屋研究室**](https://space.bilibili.com/503934057) and [**T8star-Aix**](https://space.bilibili.com/385085361) for testing the project and providing valuable feedback. *Listed in chronological order of participation.* ## Acknowledgment We thank [OpenVDN](https://github.com/OpenVDN) for [Video DeltaNet / VDN-H3](https://github.com/OpenVDN/vdn-minimax-h3) and its open-source model weights, training code and inference implementation. We thank Impossible Research for providing computation resources. We also thank [MiniMax H3](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3) for the base model and the following projects: [ComfyUI](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI), [Diffusers](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers), [SageAttention](https://github.com/thu-ml/SageAttention), the [MiniMax H3 latent upscaler](https://huggingface.co/LBH-123-AI/Minimax_h3_latent_Upscaler), the [H3 text encoder for ComfyUI](https://huggingface.co/t8star/Vdn-Minimax-H3-Comfy) and [Qt for Python](https://doc.qt.io/qtforpython-6/). ## License The code is released under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). The model weights are licensed under the [MiniMax H3 Community License](https://huggingface.co/OpenVDN/vdn-minimax-h3-edge/blob/main/LICENSE), which includes territorial and acceptable-use restrictions.

name: mailflare
description: Email for professionals and teams
readme_content:
# Mailflare A self-hosted alternative to Google Workspace. Setup **custom domain Emails**, **Calendar, Drive, Booking** and **built-in AI agents**. Self-host it on Cloudflare or Docker. **Or try [Mailflare Cloud](https://cloud.mailflare.co?ref=github) with high-deliverable emails** from $4​ [![Deploy to Cloudflare](https://deploy.workers.cloudflare.com/button)](https://deploy.workers.cloudflare.com/?url=https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare) ## Screenshots

Inbox
Domains
Mailboxes

Calendar
Booking
Drive
## Features ### Apps - **Email**: Custom domain mailboxes, personal or shared, with access you control. Send and receive with Cloudflare Email, Resend or Amazon SES. - **Routing rules**: Store, forward, reject or sort incoming mail, including a one-rule filter for newsletters and promotions. - **Calendar**: Repeating events with time zones. Attendees get email invitations. - **Booking**: Share a public link so anyone can book a free time on your calendar. - **Drive**: Store and share files. - **AI agents**: Search mail, draft replies and manage events. Connect other AI tools over MCP. ### Technical - **Databases**: Cloudflare D1 (default), PostgreSQL, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, or a local SQLite file. Set `DATABASE_URL` to switch. Works with Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale, TiDB and more. See [Databases](docs/databases.md). - **File storage**: Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3. - **Hosting**: Cloudflare Workers or a single Docker container. - **Admin**: Users, API keys, webhooks, audit logs and backups. - **Import**: Bring in mail from IMAP, Gmail Takeout, `.eml` and `.mbox` files, and Google Calendar events, Google Contacts and Google Drive files from Takeout. See [Importing from Google Takeout](docs/import.md). Mailflare currently supports 34 languages, including English, Português (Brasil), Português (Portugal), Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Nederlands, Polski, Українська, Русский, Türkçe, 中文（简体）, 日本語, 한국어, Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu, Tiếng Việt, ไทย, हिन्दी, বাংলা, मराठी, తెలుగు, தமிழ், ગુજરાતી, ಕನ್ನಡ, മലയാളം, ਪੰਜਾਬੀ, සිංහල, Kiswahili, Hausa, plus العربية, اردو and فارسی (right-to-left). ## Cost You can receive and send mail for free. - **Receiving**: Cloudflare Email Routing is free. - **Sending**: Use the free tier of Resend (3,000 emails a month) or Amazon SES. Cloudflare's own sending needs the $5/month Paid Worker plan. New Amazon SES accounts start in a sandbox. Ask AWS for production access to lift it. Prices change, so check [Resend](https://resend.com/pricing), [Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/) and [Cloudflare](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/). ## Deploy 1. **Deploy the app.** Click **Deploy to Cloudflare**. Keep the app name `mailflare`, or it will break. 2. **Finish setup.** Open the app at `/setup` and create your admin account. 3. **Connect a domain.** Add a domain from the same Cloudflare account, then create your first mailbox. > **`CF_TOKEN` is required.** Create a scoped [Cloudflare API token](https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare/issues/24#issuecomment-5523686105) with these permissions: > > - All accounts: Email Sending:Edit, DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Addresses:Edit > - All zones: DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Rules:Edit, Zone Settings:Edit, DNS:Edit More options: [deployment guide](docs/deployment.md). ### Deploy with an AI agent Paste this into an AI agent that has terminal access (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar): ```text Install Mailflare for me from https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare on my Cloudflare account. 1. Read README.md, docs/deployment.md and wrangler.jsonc first. 2. Ask me for my Cloudflare account ID and two API tokens, using a secret input: a deploy token (for Wrangler) and a runtime token (the Worker secret CF_TOKEN). Never print them, commit them, or pass them as command arguments. 3. Keep the Worker name exactly "mailflare". Create or reuse the D1 database "mailflare", the R2 bucket "mailflare-raw", and the queues "mailflare-inbound", "mailflare-outbound" and "mailflare-agent". 4. Install dependencies, run `npm run deploy`, and set CF_TOKEN as a Worker secret. Do not run remote database migrations yourself. The /setup page does that. 5. Give me the app URL and anything I still need to do. I will open /setup, create the admin account and connect my domain. ``` Token permissions and more options: [deployment guide](docs/deployment.md#deploy-with-an-ai-coding-agent). ### Self-host with Docker Runs as one container on any server, with SQLite and local files. ```bash cp .env.docker.example .env.docker docker compose up -d --build ``` Or skip the build and run the prebuilt image: `docker compose -f docker-compose.image.yml up -d`. See [self-hosting](docs/self-hosting.md). ## Local development ```bash cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars npm install npm run db:migrate:local npm run dev ``` Add your Cloudflare credentials to `.dev.vars`, then open [localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). Run `npm run db:seed` to load sample data. - `npm run build`: build the Worker - `npm run deploy`: build and deploy - `npm run lint`: lint and type check A schema change needs a migration for each database type. See [Databases](docs/databases.md#migrations). ## Documentation - [Deployment and configuration](docs/deployment.md) - [Databases](docs/databases.md) - [Sending and receiving providers](docs/providers.md) - [API and integrations](docs/api.md) - [Email assistant and MCP](docs/email-assistant-and-mcp.md) - [Importing from Google Takeout](docs/import.md) - [Adding a language](docs/localization.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) ## License See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

readme_content:
# CodeGraph Already installed? Run `codegraph upgrade` Follow [@getcodegraph](https://x.com/getcodegraph) on X for updates. ### Supercharge Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes Agent, Gemini, Antigravity, Kiro, GitHub Copilot, and more with Semantic Code Intelligence **The fastest complete code graph · surgical context · built for how agents actually work · 100% local**   **Kernel powered by Rust** ### [Documentation & Website →](https://colbymchenry.github.io/codegraph/) [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@colbymchenry/codegraph.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@colbymchenry/codegraph) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![Antigravity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Antigravity-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![Kiro](https://img.shields.io/badge/Kiro-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![GitHub Copilot](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub_Copilot-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![IBM Bob](https://img.shields.io/badge/IBM_Bob-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![Factory Droid](https://img.shields.io/badge/Factory_Droid-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![Windsurf](https://img.shields.io/badge/Windsurf-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![Qwen Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/Qwen_Code-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![DeepSeek Harness](https://img.shields.io/badge/DeepSeek_Harness-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![Grok Build](https://img.shields.io/badge/Grok_Build-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![Kimi Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/Kimi_Code-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![Qoder](https://img.shields.io/badge/Qoder-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents) [![Pi](https://img.shields.io/badge/Pi-supported-blueviolet.svg)](#supported-agents)
**The CodeGraph platform is coming** — for every PR, know exactly what to test, what could break, which flows are affected, and whether business logic is compromised. Get early beta access to the hosted product · getcodegraph.com
## Contents - [Get Started](#get-started) - [Language Support](#language-support) - [Why CodeGraph?](#why-codegraph) - [Key Features](#key-features) - [Framework-aware Routes](#framework-aware-routes) - [Mixed iOS / React Native / Expo bridging](#mixed-ios--react-native--expo-bridging) - [Quick Start](#quick-start) - [How It Works](#how-it-works) - [CLI Reference](#cli-reference) - [MCP Tools](#mcp-tools) - [Library Usage](#library-usage) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Telemetry](#telemetry) - [Verified releases](#verified-releases) - [Supported Platforms](#supported-platforms) - [Supported Agents](#supported-agents) - [Supported Languages](#supported-languages) - [Measured cross-file coverage](#measured-cross-file-coverage) - [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) - [Contributing](#contributing) - [License](#license) ## Get Started ### 1. Install the CLI **No Node.js required** — one command grabs the right build for your OS: ```bash # macOS / Linux curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/colbymchenry/codegraph/main/install.sh | sh # Windows (PowerShell) irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/colbymchenry/codegraph/main/install.ps1 | iex ```
Already have Node? Use npm instead (works on any version) ```bash npm i -g @colbymchenry/codegraph ``` CodeGraph bundles its own runtime — nothing to compile, no native build, works the same everywhere. The installer puts `codegraph` on your PATH but **doesn't change your current shell** — open a new terminal before the next step so the command resolves. **Upgrade any time** with `codegraph upgrade` — it detects how you installed (bundle, npm, or npx) and updates in place. Add `--check` to see if an update is available, or `codegraph upgrade ` to pin one. After an upgrade, `codegraph status` and your agent tell you when a project's index was built by an older version: run `codegraph index` there to rebuild it.
### 2. Wire up your agent(s) In a **new terminal**, run the installer to connect CodeGraph to the agents you use: ```bash codegraph install ``` Detects and auto-configures Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, opencode, Hermes Agent, Gemini CLI, Antigravity IDE, Kiro, GitHub Copilot (VS Code, Copilot CLI, JetBrains IDEs), IBM Bob, Factory Droid, Windsurf, Qwen Code, DeepSeek Harness, Grok Build, Kimi Code, Qoder CLI, and Pi — wiring the CodeGraph MCP server into each. **This is the step that connects CodeGraph to your agent;** installing the CLI in step 1 does not do it on its own. It only wires up your agent — it does **not** index any code; building each project's graph is the separate `codegraph init` in step 3. (Shortcut: `npx @colbymchenry/codegraph` downloads and runs this in one go.) ### 3. Initialize each project ```bash cd your-project codegraph init ``` `codegraph init` creates the local `.codegraph/` directory and builds the full graph in the same step — one command, done.
![1_C_VYnhpys0UHrOuOgpgoyw](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f168182f-4d9a-44e0-94d7-08d018cc8a3a)
### 4. No more syncing! Auto-sync is enabled by default. CodeGraph watches the project and updates the graph on every file change — while your agent edits code, or you add, modify, or delete files. **The index is never stale, and there is nothing to re-run.** ### Uninstall Changed your mind? One command removes CodeGraph from every agent it configured **and** the CLI itself — every install it finds (standalone bundle, npm global package, launcher link), shown to you before anything is deleted: ```bash codegraph uninstall ``` Pass `--keep-cli` to remove only the agent configurations and keep the CLI installed. Reverses the installer — strips CodeGraph's MCP server config, instructions, and permissions from each configured agent. Your project indexes (`.codegraph/`) are left untouched; remove those per-project with `codegraph uninit`. Use `--target` to remove from specific agents, or `--yes` to run non-interactively. --- ## Language Support Every language below gets the same treatment — full structural extraction and cross-file resolution into one graph, no per-language setup:
